title: Instruction-following under quantization — sprint notes
content:
Quick context: ran a 2-week exploratory sprint to understand how aggressive weight/activation quantization (4-bit, mixed 3/4-bit) affects instruction-following behavior on medium-size open models (7B–13B). Goal is pragmatic: what breaks for product-level instruction flows (tool-calling, chained prompts, short-context clarifications) versus what only affects long-form generation quality.

High-level takeaways (TL;DR):
- Latency and memory win is real: 3/4-bit mixed configs reduced peak GPU memory by ~35–45% and improved end-to-end token throughput by ~18% on our test harness.
- Instruction robustness degrades unevenly: simple single-step instructions (summarize X) are fine at 4-bit; multi-step tool-calling and examples with formatting constraints degrade faster.
- Calibration and safety classifiers drift: logits and softmax temperature sensitivity change under quantization which affects n-best ranking for rerankers.
- KV-cache precision loss is the main culprit for multi-turn fidelity loss in many runs (notes below).

Setup and methodology:
- Models: forked variants of open-7B-v2 and open-13B-lite. Implemented QAT-style retrain for a couple of checkpoints; majority used post-training static quantization with learned scale (per-group 64) and outlier clipping.
- Hardware: A100 and Ampere-Edge test nodes (the latter for the latency-tail checks).
- Workloads: 200 instruction templates; split into: single-turn short (40%), multi-step with tool-calls (25%), chained clarifications (20%), low-safety-hazard prompts (15%). Also a small RAG/QA sample set for retrieval interaction.
- Metrics collected (structured CSV): exact-match on directive compliance, BLEU/ROUGE for summarization sanity checks, human pass/fail for tool-call correctness (do the right args get emitted), latency p50/p95, peak memory.

Experiment notes (raw observations):
- Single-turn summarization: 4-bit configs mostly indistinguishable to quick human checks. Auto-metrics slightly down (~2–4% relative ROUGE), but hardly noticeable.
- Tool-calling templates: notable failure modes — truncated JSON objects, missing required keys, and syntactically valid but semantically wrong argument values. Error rate increased ~3x vs fp16 baseline.
- Chained clarification flows: hallucinated additions more frequent; the model sometimes 'invented' intermediate steps when the KV-cache could not preserve earlier conditioning precisely.
- Retrieval/RAG: retrieval signals still helpful; however, exact anchoring to retrieved passages was less consistent. When we appended retrieved text with explicit markers, quantized models sometimes ignored the marker ordering.

Hypotheses and quick probes:
- Hypothesis A: Activation quantization noise accumulates across attention layers causing drift in long-range token representations. Evidence: layer-wise probe where early layers preserved answer tokens but later layers diverged in cosine similarity to fp16 hidden states.
- Hypothesis B: Mixed-precision (keep first N layers in 8-bit or fp16) recovers a lot of multi-turn behavior at small memory cost. Quick test: keeping first 3 transformer blocks at 8-bit restored ~60% of lost tool-call fidelity while only increasing memory by ~8%.
- Hypothesis C: Rounding/clipping heuristics in per-group scales generate outliers; small activation clamping helps. We saw improvements after increasing clip_percentile from 99.9 to 99.995 for a subset of cases.

Mini-experiment log (not exhaustive):
- 2029-05-04: baseline fp16 run, 200 prompts -> tool-call pass rate 92%
- 2029-05-06: 4-bit post-train quant -> pass rate 67%, p95 latency -12%
- 2029-05-09: mixed 4/8-bit (first 3 layers 8-bit) -> pass rate 81%
- 2029-05-11: QAT lightweight fine-tune (50M steps) on instruction dataset -> pass rate 86% (promising, but training cost non-trivial)

Practical mitigations (for product teams):
- Deploy hybrid-precision endpoints by routing multi-turn or tool-heavy flows to mixed configs, keep short single-turn queries on aggressive quantized pools. This aligns with Redwood's smart routing idea.
- Post-processing: simple syntactic validators for tool-calls (schema checks) catch many downstream faults even when the model emits near-correct args.
- Calibration wrappers: run small n-best reranking using fp16 scorer (cheap if only reranking a handful of candidates) to fix top-1 selection drift.
- KV-cache augmentation: store higher-precision compressed snapshots for earlier turns and replay as needed for long dialogs (might trade memory for correctness).

Open questions / next steps:
- Cost vs. fidelity sweet spot: need a structured cost model (tokens, CPU/GPU time, storage) to decide routing thresholds.
- Tool-call synthesis: can we incorporate lightweight constrained decoding that enforces required keys? How much does that slow down generation?
- Eval improvements: current human eval is small; set up a rapid raters loop and augment with targeted unit tests for common tool schemas.
- Does model architecture matter? Hypothesis: models with larger MLP ratios or different normalization behave differently under quant. Need a small cross-arch sweep.

References and crumbs (links / internal IDs):
- TinyQuant blog notes (internal): GH-PR-llm-4321 (see linked artifact)
- Slack thread: #quantization-sprint (search: "instr quant 2029")
- Internal perf dashboard: CONFLUENCE-IF-2029

Notes to self / TODOs:
- Create a compact decision tree for routing (short query vs multi-turn vs tool) and prototype in the local router.
- Add more structured tool-call unit tests (3 schemas to start).
- Run cheap cross-arch run for two more checkpoints (LlamaX-7B, OpeX-11B) in mixed configs.

Random scribbles / heuristics observed:
- "If tool args are >3 tokens and include numbers, quantized models fail more." (empirical, needs verifying)
- "Inline markers like [RETRIEVED] help but only when combined with explicit ask-to-use wording."

Final: still promising — big opportunity to reduce unit cost for many single-turn applications, but product-sensitive flows (tooling, multi-turn agents) likely need hybrid approaches or small additional engineering (validation/reranking) to be safe.

If time permits: prepare a one-pager for the Applied ML weekly (include small table of cost trade-offs and recommended routing defaults).

-- Rowan
